sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Long-term concrete pavement performance depends on adequate structural design, use of quality materials, proper construction procedures, and timely maintenance/repair; field modifications to the design should be reviewed by the original designer.
sections.body: The factors affecting long-term concrete pavement performance are broadly divided into the following categories: adequate design of pavement structure, use of quality materials, use of proper construction procedures, and timely maintenance and repair. The pavement designer controls several parameters and details that greatly impact pavement construction; these are discussed individually in the following paragraphs. When there is a conflict between design requirements and field conditions, any modifications to the design to accommodate field conditions should be reviewed by the original designer to ensure the modifications comply with the original design intent.
key_points: Four broad categories drive long-term performance: design, material quality, construction procedures, maintenance/repair
The pavement designer controls parameters that strongly affect construction
Field modifications to the design must be reviewed by the original designer to preserve design intent
sections.applicability: Frames the chapter's purpose: connecting design decisions to construction outcomes for concrete pavements.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Airfield pavement design procedures are in UFC 3-260-02; other concrete pavement (roads/parking) design procedures are in UFC 3-250-01. This section introduces the design-related considerations elaborated in the following subsections.
sections.body: Design procedures for airfield pavements are described in UFC 3-260-02, Pavement Design for Airfields. Design procedures for other concrete pavements are described in UFC 3-250-01, Pavement Design for Roads and Parking Areas.
key_points: Airfield pavement design: UFC 3-260-02
Road/parking pavement design: UFC 3-250-01
This UFC (3-250-04) governs construction practice, not the thickness design procedure itself
sections.applicability: Directs the reader to the correct companion design UFC before applying this construction-practice document.

sections.title: Pavement Foundation
sections.summary: Designers must provide a firm foundation for construction traffic and equipment; UFC 3-260-02 mandates base courses on pumping-susceptible subgrades, and a base course may also be warranted on SM/SC/GC/SP soils that are unstable under wet construction traffic.
sections.body: Provide a firm foundation to support concrete construction activities, such as slipform pavers, forms, concrete delivery truck traffic, and other heavy vehicles or equipment. Designers will consider the anticipated field soil support and moisture conditions during construction and select base courses to support concrete placement activities. UFC 3-260-02 mandates use of base courses on pumping susceptible subgrade soils, which generally include the silts and clays that are the most troublesome during construction. However, the designer may include a base course to ensure a viable construction platform for soils such as those classified as SM, SC, GC, or SP by the Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM D2487), since these may not be stable under construction traffic or during wet construction conditions. A designer assesses the characteristics of the subgrade soil at a project location to determine whether a base course is required to support construction activities. Extend base courses far enough beyond the edge of the pavement to accommodate construction activities such as slipform paver tracks or to provide space to place and anchor forms. Only use stabilized bases on airfields when there is a specific need, such as lack of suitable local base material, an all-weather construction platform, or other structural requirements; designers working on design-build contracts must be made aware of this difference at initial design meetings.
key_points: UFC 3-260-02 mandates base courses over pumping-susceptible (silt/clay) subgrades
Base course may also be warranted for USCS SM/SC/GC/SP soils unstable under wet construction traffic
Extend base courses beyond the pavement edge for paver tracks / form anchoring
Stabilized bases on airfields are used only when specifically needed (material scarcity, all-weather platform, structural requirement)
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting/sizing a base course to serve as a stable construction platform, not only as the final design layer.

sections.title: Concrete Strength
sections.summary: Design flexural strength is traditionally the 90-day ASTM C78/CRD-C 16 value, specified between 600 and 700 psi (4136-4826 kPa) for military airfields without prior TSPDWG approval; designers must balance early-opening strength needs against workability/durability.
sections.body: Traditionally, calculating the design strength for pavement thickness equates to the ASTM C78/CRD-C 16 flexural strength at 90 days. While modern concrete mixtures can achieve very high strength, this can introduce adverse setting and handling characteristics or shrinkage. Therefore, specify no flexural strength less than 600 psi (4136 kPa) or greater than 700 psi (4826 kPa) for military airfields without prior approval from the TSPDWG. Specifying a 90-day strength allowed designers to take advantage of strength gains between 28 and 90 days before allowing traffic or for minimal traffic; most modern portland cement chemistry and grinding produce very modest strength increases between 28 and 90 days, however concretes using supplementary cementitious materials such as fly ash and GGBF slag can gain substantial strength after 28 days. Projects often require reopening pavement to traffic early. A designer balances the desired strength, the time to achieve this strength, and other factors such as durability, against specific project requirements. For pavement that must open early to traffic, the designer should calculate the effect of the limited early-age traffic on the total pavement life to select reasonable strengths before allowing traffic; simply requiring the normal 90-day strength at some very early age can generate a concrete mixture possessing troublesome working characteristics.
key_points: Design basis: ASTM C78/CRD-C 16 flexural strength at 90 days (traditional)
Specified flexural strength range for military airfields: 600-700 psi (4136-4826 kPa) without prior TSPDWG approval
Mixes with supplementary cementitious materials (fly ash, GGBF slag) gain more strength between 28 and 90 days than plain portland cement
Forcing normal 90-day strength at an early age can create mixtures with poor working characteristics
sections.applicability: Governs setting the specified flexural strength and reconciling it with early-opening / fast-track schedule needs.

sections.title: Pavement Dimensions
sections.summary: Airfield concrete pavements are normally jointed plain concrete, sized on mixed aircraft loadings; heavy-traffic slabs range 400-500 mm (16-20 in.) thick with 4.6-6.2 m (15-20 ft) joint spacing, light-traffic slabs 125-300 mm (5-12 in.) with 2.4-4.6 m (8-15 ft) spacing; maximum slab size is limited to 6.1 m (20 ft) since spacing >= 7.6 m (25 ft) increases uncontrolled-cracking risk.
sections.body: Concrete pavements for any application are normally jointed plain concrete pavements; only reinforce odd-shaped slabs or for special circumstances such as continuously reinforced concrete. Airport concrete pavements are typically designed on the basis of mixed aircraft loadings to minimize maintenance service for multiple decades, and are designed on the basis of expected aircraft repetitions over the design period. For many airfield pavements, the concrete thickness may range from 400 to 500 mm (16 to 20 in.) and transverse joint spacing may range from 4.6 to 6.2 m (15 to 20 ft); typical longitudinal joint spacing can also range from 4.6 to 6.2 m (15 to 20 ft). Current practice uses dowel bars for load transfer in all longitudinal construction joints. For concrete pavements subjected to only light aircraft loads, slab thickness may range from 125 to 300 mm (5 to 12 in.) and transverse and longitudinal joint spacing may range from 2.4 to 4.6 m (8 to 15 ft). Slab dimensions in design manuals are set to minimize curling stresses from non-load-associated factors; failure to adhere to these limits leads to unwanted cracking due to the combined effect of curling stresses and load-related flexural stresses. For these reasons, common practice limits the maximum slab size to 6.1 m (20 ft), as research shows that slab joint spacing equal to or greater than 7.6 m (25 ft) increases the risk of uncontrolled cracking.
key_points: Airfield concrete pavements are normally jointed plain concrete; reinforcement reserved for odd-shaped slabs or continuously reinforced concrete
Heavy-load slabs: thickness 400-500 mm (16-20 in.), joint spacing 4.6-6.2 m (15-20 ft) both directions
Light-load slabs: thickness 125-300 mm (5-12 in.), joint spacing 2.4-4.6 m (8-15 ft)
Current practice: dowel bars for load transfer at all longitudinal construction joints
Maximum practical slab size limited to 6.1 m (20 ft); spacing >= 7.6 m (25 ft) raises uncontrolled-cracking risk
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting slab thickness and joint spacing ranges consistent with load category and curling-stress control.

sections.title: Legacy Slabs
sections.summary: Older airfield pavements with 7.6 m (25 ft) slabs can create mismatched joints against new construction sized to current limits; designers should develop cost-effective jointing/repair details (e.g. expansion joints, partial reinforcement) that mitigate the mismatch, per UFC 3-260-02.
sections.body: On older airfield pavements with 7.6 m (25 ft) slabs, strict adherence to current slab-size policy may create mismatched slab joints. Where joint patterns of abutting pavement facilities do not match, partial reinforcement of slabs may be necessary; using reinforcement at mismatched joints in such junctures is based upon the type of joint between the two pavement sections. Designers should develop repair projects with a cost-effective joint pattern that minimizes and mitigates mismatch between larger legacy slabs and smaller new slabs by incorporating appropriate protective measures, such as expansion joints or reinforcing. See further discussion in UFC 3-260-02.
key_points: Legacy 7.6 m (25 ft) slabs commonly mismatch joints against new, smaller-slab construction
Partial reinforcement at mismatched joints depends on the joint type between the two pavement sections
Mitigation options include expansion joints and slab reinforcement
See UFC 3-260-02 for further discussion
sections.applicability: Applies to repair/tie-in projects where new pavement must join existing legacy slabs of a different joint pattern.

sections.title: Design Process
sections.summary: The layer directly under the slab is termed 'base' and the layer between base and subgrade is 'subbase'; the overall concrete pavement design process follows the sequential steps elaborated in the following subsections.
sections.body: The terms 'base' and 'subbase' often designate the layer directly under the concrete slab; in this UFC, the layer immediately below the slab is called the base, and the layer between the base and the subgrade is called the subbase. The overall process of designing a concrete pavement involves the sequential steps covered in the following subsections: soil investigation, evaluating subgrade support at design grade, designing the pavement section, selecting the jointing plan, developing plans and specifications, identifying critical design features, and accounting for construction variability.
key_points: This UFC's terminology: 'base' = layer directly under the slab; 'subbase' = layer between base and subgrade
Design process proceeds through soil investigation -> subgrade evaluation -> pavement section design -> jointing plan -> plans/specifications
sections.applicability: Establishes base/subbase terminology and the overall sequence of the concrete pavement design process.

sections.title: Soil Investigation
sections.summary: Soil borings determine subsurface strata properties and depth to groundwater; soil samples are obtained for classification and laboratory testing per UFC 3-260-02.
sections.body: Soil borings determine the properties of the subsurface strata and depth to groundwater. Soil samples are obtained for soil classification and laboratory testing (see UFC 3-260-02).
key_points: Soil borings establish subsurface stratigraphy and groundwater depth
Samples support classification and laboratory testing per UFC 3-260-02
sections.applicability: First step of the design process, providing the subsurface data needed for later steps.

sections.title: Evaluate Subgrade Support at Design Grade
sections.summary: The soil investigation results indicate subgrade conditions at and below the finished design grade elevation.
sections.body: The information from the soil investigation indicates the subgrade conditions at and below the design grade.
key_points: Subgrade support is evaluated at and below the finished design grade elevation, using the soil investigation results
sections.applicability: Second step of the design process, translating boring data into a subgrade support assessment at grade.

sections.title: Design Pavement Section
sections.summary: After determining base type (stabilized or non-stabilized) and thickness, the appropriate design procedure calculates the required PCC pavement thickness.
sections.body: After determining the appropriate base type (i.e., stabilized or non-stabilized) and thickness, use the appropriate design procedure to calculate the required PCC pavement thickness.
key_points: Base type (stabilized vs. non-stabilized) and thickness are determined before calculating slab thickness
The PCC thickness is calculated with the applicable design procedure (UFC 3-260-02 or UFC 3-250-01)
sections.applicability: Third step of the design process: converting base/subgrade decisions into a required slab thickness.

sections.title: Select Jointing Plan
sections.summary: Longitudinal and transverse joint details are developed from the calculated slab dimensions, including proper construction details for joints and transition slabs tying into existing pavements.
sections.body: Develop appropriate longitudinal and transverse joint details based on the calculated slab dimensions. Proper construction details are required for joints and transition slabs that tie in to existing pavements.
key_points: Joint layout follows directly from the calculated slab dimensions
Transition-slab tie-ins to existing pavement need their own construction details
sections.applicability: Fourth step of the design process: converting slab dimensions into an actual joint layout.

sections.title: Develop Plans and Specifications
sections.summary: The design details are further developed into complete construction plans and specifications.
sections.body: Further develop the design details into complete plans and specifications. This step turns the calculated pavement section and jointing plan into bid-ready construction documents.
key_points: Design details are finalized into complete plans and specifications for construction
This step follows selection of the jointing plan and precedes construction procurement
sections.applicability: Fifth step of the design process, producing the bid-ready construction documents.

sections.title: Critical Design Features
sections.summary: Long-term concrete pavement performance depends on a defined set of critical design features spanning subgrade/base uniformity, PCC layer thickness and properties (uniformity, workability, strength, durability), jointing details, slab dimensions, load transfer, and joint sealing.
sections.body: Critical design features that influence long-term concrete pavement performance include: subgrade support uniformity and stability; base and subbase uniformity (type and thickness), including drainage; PCC pavement layer thickness; PCC properties as specified; uniformity (ability of concrete to produce consistent properties); workability (ability of concrete to be placed, consolidated, and finished); strength (ability of concrete to support traffic and environmental conditions); durability (ability of concrete to provide long-term service); jointing details; slab dimensions; load transfer at joints; and joint sealing provisions.
key_points: Subgrade/base uniformity and stability, including drainage
PCC layer thickness and specified properties: uniformity, workability, strength, durability
Jointing details, slab dimensions, load transfer at joints, and joint sealing provisions
sections.applicability: Serves as a checklist of the design features that most strongly govern long-term pavement performance.

sections.title: Construction Variability
sections.summary: Variability in key design-element properties significantly affects pavement performance; the design engineer sets acceptable parameters, quality management plans control construction variability, and stacking multiple marginal features (design or construction) tends to produce premature failure or poor lifetime performance.
sections.body: Throughout the design process, recognize that variability in the properties of key design elements significantly affects pavement performance. While some variability is unavoidable, excessive variability during construction induces random pavement performance and higher contractor costs. Make effective use of quality management plans to control construction variability. For each project, the design engineer establishes the acceptable parameters for each design variable, and construction work must meet or exceed the specified quality. Typically, when several marginal features are incorporated into a pavement structure through a design deficiency, poor construction techniques, or a combination thereof, premature failure results or the pavement performs poorly throughout its service life.
key_points: Excessive construction variability produces random performance and higher contractor costs
Quality management plans are the primary tool for controlling construction variability
The design engineer sets the acceptable parameter range for each design variable
Stacking several marginal features (design and/or construction) tends to cause premature failure or poor lifetime performance
sections.applicability: Applies throughout design and construction to justify quality-management controls on variability.

sections.title: Critical Construction Operations
sections.summary: Introduces the specific construction operations most critical to pavement performance, each cross-referenced to the chapter that covers it in detail: grading, jointing, subgrade/subbase/base quality, PCC strength, durability, curing, finishability, and paver operation.
sections.body: Examples of critical construction operations include the operations covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Introduces the critical-construction-operations list expanded in the following subsections
sections.applicability: Bridges from design considerations to the construction-practice chapters that follow.

sections.title: Grading
sections.summary: Proper grading facilitates drainage and placement of successive layers; grading issues are discussed in Chapters 4, 5, and 6.
sections.body: Grading is important. Proper grading facilitates drainage and placement of successive layers. Grading issues are discussed in Chapters 4, 5, and 6.
key_points: Proper grading enables drainage and correct placement of successive pavement layers
Grading is covered in Chapters 4 (subgrade), 5 (base/subbase), and 6 (paving preparation)
sections.applicability: Cross-references the chapters that detail grading practice for subgrade, base/subbase, and paving preparation.

sections.title: Jointing
sections.summary: Jointing controls slab cracking; shallow or late sawing, or misaligned/bonded dowel bars, can defeat joint function and cause random cracking that reduces load capacity. Joint sawing, load transfer, and sealing practices are discussed in Chapter 9.
sections.body: Jointing controls slab cracking, which minimizes the potential for random cracking. Random cracking is a maintenance concern and can reduce the load capacity of pavement. Shallow joint sawing and late sawing can induce random cracking. If dowel bars are misaligned or bonded to the concrete, joints do not function and adjacent slab panels can develop random cracking. Joint sawing, load transfer, and joint sealing practices are discussed in Chapter 9.
key_points: Random cracking (from poor jointing) is a maintenance concern and reduces pavement load capacity
Shallow or late sawcutting can induce random cracking
Misaligned or bonded dowel bars defeat joint function and can trigger random cracking in adjacent slabs
Detailed joint sawing/load-transfer/sealing practice is in Chapter 9
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapter 9 for the construction practices that keep joints functioning as intended.

sections.title: Subgrade, Subbase, and Base Quality
sections.summary: Compromised compaction of subgrade, subbase, or base can cause excessive deflection under aircraft loading and corner cracking; construction practices for these layers are presented in Chapters 4 and 5.
sections.body: If the compaction of the subgrade, subbase, and base is compromised, the pavement may deflect excessively under aircraft loading and develop corner cracking. Subgrade, subbase, and base construction practices are presented in Chapters 4 and 5, respectively.
key_points: Compromised subgrade/subbase/base compaction can cause excessive deflection and corner cracking under aircraft loading
Detailed construction practices are in Chapter 4 (subgrade) and Chapter 5 (base/subbase)
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapters 4 and 5 for the foundation-layer construction practices behind pavement performance.

sections.title: PCC Strength
sections.summary: Low-strength concrete results in early fatigue cracking; typical 28-day airfield flexural strength is 4,100-5,200 kPa (600-750 psi), with earlier strength possibly required for fast-track construction. Concrete practices including strength requirements are discussed in Chapters 6 and 7.
sections.body: Low-strength concrete results in early fatigue cracking of the pavement. Concrete flexural strength at 28 days for airfield paving is typically 4,100 to 5,200 kPa (600 to 750 psi). For fast-track construction, these strength levels may be required earlier. Concrete practices, including strength requirements, are discussed in Chapters 6 and 7.
key_points: Low-strength concrete causes early fatigue cracking
Typical 28-day airfield flexural strength: 4,100-5,200 kPa (600-750 psi)
Fast-track construction may require these strength levels at an earlier age
Detailed concrete mixture practices are in Chapters 6 and 7
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapters 6 and 7 for concrete mixture practice governing strength gain and fatigue resistance.

sections.title: Concrete Durability
sections.summary: Concrete that is not durable, due to poor or reactive materials, a poor air-void system, or over-finishing, deteriorates prematurely; durability issues are discussed in Chapters 7 and 8.
sections.body: Concrete that is not durable (a result of poor or reactive materials, a poor air-void system, or due to over-finishing) deteriorates prematurely. Concrete durability issues are discussed in Chapters 7 and 8.
key_points: Premature deterioration commonly traces to poor/reactive materials, a poor air-void system, or over-finishing
Durability issues are addressed in Chapters 7 (mixture) and 8 (placement/finishing/curing)
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapters 7 and 8 for the material and construction causes of durability problems.

sections.title: Concrete Curing
sections.summary: Improperly cured concrete can deteriorate prematurely and generate early-age spalling; Chapter 8 discusses concrete curing practices.
sections.body: Improperly cured concrete can deteriorate prematurely and generate early age spalling. Chapter 8 discusses concrete curing practices.
key_points: Improper curing causes premature deterioration and early-age spalling
Curing practice is detailed in Chapter 8
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapter 8 for curing practice and its role in preventing early-age spalling.

sections.title: Concrete Finishability
sections.summary: Concrete that is over-finished or requires excessive manipulation to achieve an acceptable finish deteriorates prematurely and may generate poor surface conditions; see Chapter 8.
sections.body: Concrete that is over-finished or requires excessive manipulation to provide an acceptable finish deteriorates prematurely. Poorly finished concrete may also generate poor surface conditions. See Chapter 8.
key_points: Over-finishing or excessive manipulation causes premature deterioration and poor surface conditions
Finishing practice is detailed in Chapter 8
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapter 8 for finishing practice that avoids over-manipulation of the concrete surface.

sections.title: Paver Operation
sections.summary: Paver operations significantly impact pavement smoothness and in-place concrete quality; Chapter 8 discusses paver operation practices.
sections.body: Paver operations significantly impact pavement smoothness and in-place concrete quality. Chapter 8 discusses paver operation practices.
key_points: Paver operation strongly affects both surface smoothness and in-place concrete quality
Paver operation practice is detailed in Chapter 8
sections.applicability: Cross-references Chapter 8 for paver operation practice affecting smoothness and concrete quality.
